meta.blurb: Amara cannot sleep, because her head is full of things she must not forget. One evening she sits down with a pen and a large blank sheet and writes down all of it. A simple system turns the pile into calm.
meta.bible: Amara: a school office manager and parent whose mind is full of things to remember. Dev: a university student with a long essay to write. The book speaks to "you" and uses these two as examples. Key ideas, in the book's own words: one trusted place to collect everything; sorting each item; the first small step; a waiting list; a clean calendar; a short daily look; an end-of-week tidy held on Friday afternoon; an ideas page; a closing note at the end of the work day. Research is real and hedged: working memory is limited and the exact number is debated; one set of experiments found that a plan quiets an unfinished goal; one small sleep study found that writing a to-do list before bed helped people fall asleep faster. Mondays: the day of one routine decision. Kofi: Amara's partner, a bus driver who works early shifts. Zuri: their daughter, nine years old, who is learning to swim. Ines: Amara's neighbour, a hospital nurse who keeps a small notebook in her pocket. Hana: the head teacher of the school where Amara works. Mr Bell: the school caretaker. Lucas: Dev's friend and flatmate. Dr Moyo: Dev's essay tutor. Amara's town has a small school, a pharmacy, a library and a post office. The school trip form, the dentist, the leak under the kitchen sink, Zuri's swimming kit and a gift for Amara's mother are the first things on her mind. Fixed facts of the story: Amara empties her head on a Sunday evening and finds more than a hundred items; her notebook has a plain hard cover; she holds her end-of-week tidy on Friday afternoon with a lamp and a cup of tea; her short daily look is five minutes at the kitchen table in the morning; Dev's essay is due in three weeks and he finishes it early. Voice and tone: calm, kind, practical and reassuring, one clear idea or step in each beat, building to a final takeaway. More fixed facts: Amara's mother has a birthday in about two weeks, and Amara posts her gift in a parcel from the post office. The plumber comes on the day he promised, after Amara reminds him. Zuri's swimming lesson is on Saturday; her instructor helps her float. Dev's essay is about how rivers shaped the first cities; his tutor Dr Moyo tells him to write the introduction last. Dev writes each morning from nine to eleven in the library. Kofi lays out his uniform the night before and records voice notes on his break at the bus depot. Ines notes ward supplies and her own errands in her pocket notebook. Hana is calm and fair. Amara's weekly meal plan is made on Monday and stuck to the fridge with a magnet; Zuri's swim bag is packed on Friday evening. Amara shows Ines the five steps: collect, sort, choose, review, rest. Aunt Mary: Amara's aunt, to whom she writes a card. Zuri's swimming teacher is warm and sensible.

B1B2: Amara lies in bed at midnight, and her mind will not stop. It keeps listing everything she must do, buy, send and remember tomorrow.
Unable to sleep, Amara creeps down to the kitchen and pours a glass of water. The light from the fridge falls on a school trip form stuck there with a magnet.
The form must be signed and returned by Friday, and she has not even read it properly. Then she remembers that she also has to call the dentist for Zuri.
A slow drip sounds from under the sink, where a bowl is catching water from a small leak. Amara has meant to phone a plumber for two weeks, but something always gets in the way.
By the front door, Zuri's swim bag is open and half empty, and her goggles are nowhere to be seen. The lesson is on Saturday, and Zuri will be very upset without them.
Her mother's birthday is only two weeks away, and Amara has no idea what to give her. She promised herself that she would think of something early this year.
Upstairs, Kofi is sleeping deeply, because his alarm will ring at half past four for the early bus. Amara does not want to wake him, so she sits alone with her long list of worries.
The next day at the school office, Amara is so tired that she forgets to send an important email. Nothing terrible happens, but the mistake frightens her, because it is not like her.
She also forgot to tell Mr Bell, the caretaker, about a window lock that no longer closes. He only smiles and says that nobody can keep every little thing in their head.

That evening, Amara tells her neighbour Ines about her sleepless nights over the garden fence. Ines, who is a hospital nurse, takes a small notebook from her pocket and says she has a simple way to keep her head clear.
Your mind is wonderful at having ideas and solving problems. It is a poor storage room, however, and it will lose things at the worst moments.
Psychologists have found that we can hold only a handful of things in mind at the same moment. The exact number is still debated, but it is much smaller than a to-do list.
At night, the world becomes quiet, and nothing else is asking for your attention. That is exactly when your mind starts to replay every forgotten job.
Imagine a computer with dozens of windows open at once. It still works, but it runs slowly, and the same is true of a mind that is trying to remember everything.
Unfinished jobs nag at us, even when we are busy with something else. In some well-known experiments, people kept thinking about tasks that they had not completed.

The same experiments suggested something hopeful: making a specific plan for an unfinished job seemed to quiet the nagging. The job did not need to be done, and it only needed to be written down with a next step.
Every time you tell yourself to remember something, you spend a little of your attention. A hundred small promises of this kind can leave you tired before the day has even begun.
A mind will only let go of a worry when it truly believes that something else will remember it. A friend's promise works in the same way, because you stop repeating it once you trust the person.
A trusted place must be with you wherever you go, and it must be easy to use. Above all, you must look at it often, or your mind will never believe it.
After Ines's advice, Amara decides to run an experiment. She circles Sunday evening on the calendar and promises herself one quiet hour with a pen and some paper.
Ines pulls a small, worn notebook from the pocket of her uniform. Between her tasks on the ward, she says, she writes down anything she must not forget.
Many people keep notes on sticky papers, envelopes, a phone and their memory all at once. If your notes are in five places, you will never trust any of them, so choose one.
The next morning, Amara walks to the post office and buys a plain notebook with a hard cover. She wants something simple, because she has no wish to spend time choosing a fancy one.
Dev, a university student, prefers an app on his phone. He says that it is always with him, and it never gets lost in the bottom of his bag.
Some people love paper and others prefer an app. Either way works, as long as you can reach it quickly and you really use it.
Before you choose, ask yourself two honest questions about the tool. Will it be with me every day, and will I truly open it when I need it?
Amara fixes a pen to the cover with a loop of string. Now she can never say that she had no pen at the moment when an idea came.
Zuri finds the notebook on the kitchen table and draws a tiny fish inside the front cover. She says that it is a brain for the table, and Amara decides that it is a very good name.
At breakfast, Kofi asks how the idea actually works, and Amara explains with her hands. He looks for a flaw, because he is a careful man, but in the end he can only nod.
Amara hangs the notebook from a hook by the front door, next to her coat. Its home is fixed, so she will never have to hunt for it in the morning.
On Sunday evening, Kofi puts Zuri to bed, and Amara sits down at the kitchen table. She has a pen, a cup of tea, a large sheet of paper and one whole hour.
The rule is simple: write down everything that is on your mind. Do not sort, judge or solve anything yet, because that comes later.
She begins with the things that have kept her awake, such as the school trip form, the dentist and the leak. Once they are on the page, she feels her shoulders drop a little.
Next come the jobs from work, both big and small. She writes about the paper for the office, the letters for parents, the window lock and a meeting that she must prepare for.

Then she thinks of home and writes a line for the washing, the bills, the food and the shoes that Zuri has outgrown. The page fills quickly, and some lines are so small that she nearly leaves them out.
Tiny jobs deserve a place too, because the mind keeps all of them. She adds a new light bulb, a library book that is overdue and a parcel that must go to the post office.

Amara also writes her worries and her wishes, because they take up space in her head just like tasks. She writes that Zuri is afraid of deep water, and that she would love to paint the hall a soft green.
When her ideas dry up, she walks slowly through the house and looks into every room with her pen ready. Each cupboard, shelf and corner reminds her of something that she had completely forgotten.
At last, Amara stops writing and counts the lines on her sheet, which is full to the edges. She has more than a hundred items, and she holds up the page in surprise.
The strange thing is that the long list feels lighter on paper than it did in her head. Sorting it will come next, but for tonight it is enough that everything is out of her mind.
From Monday, Amara writes things down the moment they come to her. A note takes ten seconds, and it frees her mind to carry on.
While she waits at the bus stop with Zuri, Amara suddenly remembers a prescription at the pharmacy. She takes out her notebook and writes it down in ten seconds, and then she smiles at the bus.
Amara keeps a small pad and a pen in her handbag and in the pocket of her coat. The habit only works if the pen is there at the very moment when the thought arrives.
Write down everything, even tiny things and things that you may never actually do. It costs almost nothing to write a line, and deciding later is far easier than trying to remember.
Write enough words so that you will understand the note a week from now. The word gift tells you very little, but gift for Mum, something warm tells you exactly what to do.
Dev goes to a crowded lecture and hears a surprising idea for his essay. Instead of trying to keep it in his head, he types it into his phone and goes on listening.
Kofi cannot write while he is driving, of course, so he waits until his break at the bus depot. Then he speaks his thoughts into his phone, and later he copies them into the notebook.
Ines hurries along a hospital corridor, but she still finds a moment to write a note with the pen from her pocket. She notes the supplies that the ward needs, and her own errands too.
At two in the morning, Amara wakes and remembers something that she did not write down. It is a small thing, but the sleepless hour that follows teaches her a lesson that no book could.
This habit is the foundation of the whole method. Whatever comes into your mind, whether it is large, small, serious or silly, goes straight into the notebook.
A long list is not yet a plan, and it can feel just as heavy as a full head. On Monday evening, Amara sits down to sort it, one line at a time.
For each item, Amara asks a simple question: is there anything I actually need to do about this? Sometimes the honest answer is simply no, and that is a perfectly good answer.
If the answer is no, she may throw the note away. She tears out a line about buying a new kettle, because the old one works perfectly well.
Some items are not jobs but pleasant ideas for the future, such as a pottery class, a knitting lesson or a trip to the sea. Amara copies them onto one page, which she calls her ideas page.
The ideas page does not need to be read every day, because it is not urgent. Amara decides to look at it once a week, when she has time to dream a little.
Certain notes are not jobs at all, but facts that she may need to look up one day. The times of Zuri's swimming lessons, for example, belong in a folder and not on a list.
Amara clears a drawer in the hall and puts in a few folders with clear names, such as tickets, bills and manuals. Anything she only needs to look up goes there, so that her lists stay clean.
By the end of the evening, Amara has thrown away about twenty items from the sheet. She is surprised by how much lighter she feels, as if she had cleared a crowded cupboard.
Dev sorts his list of forty items into three piles on his desk. Twelve are about the essay, six are ideas for later, and the rest he happily throws away.
At the end, Amara has three small stacks on the table: things to do, ideas and things to keep. The first stack is much shorter than the original list, and every item in it needs a step.
On her list, the word dentist sits there like a small cloud. It does not tell her what to do, so every time she reads it she feels worried and does nothing.
The cure is to ask one question about each item: what is the very first thing that I could physically do? The answer is usually smaller and easier than you expect.
Begin every step with an action word, such as call, write, buy or ask. A note that says dentist is only a worry, but call the dentist is a job.
Amara goes through the list again and rewrites ten unclear notes as clear steps. Dentist becomes call the dentist, and gift becomes ask Kofi for ideas.
If a step still feels heavy, make it even smaller. Instead of booking the dentist, Amara writes find the dentist's phone number, and it suddenly seems easy.
For the leak, the first step is not to fix it, because Amara cannot do that herself. She writes find a plumber's number, and then she adds call him at lunch.
Zuri's swimming kit also becomes one small step, which is to look in the swim bag. If the goggles are not there, the next step will be clear, and not before.
Amara has no idea what to buy her mother, so she does not write buy a present. She writes ask Kofi for two ideas, and that is a step that she can finish tonight.
Many steps take only a minute or two, so Amara gathers them and does them in one short burst. On Tuesday morning she finishes three tiny jobs in a row before the kettle has even boiled.
With a bold pen, Amara crosses a finished job off her list. The line is small, but each one proves that the method works, and she feels a quiet pleasure in drawing it.
The plumber says that he will come next week, but he does not give a day. Amara thanks him, then worries that he will forget, and that she will forget too.
Sometimes the next step belongs to someone else entirely. Keep a waiting list for everything that other people have promised or still owe you.
Write down what you are waiting for, who owes it and the date you asked. Three short words are enough, such as plumber, visit, Monday.
Without a list, you carry each waiting thing in your head, and it nags you just like a task. Writing it down lets you stop thinking about it until the date comes.
On Friday afternoon, Amara reads her waiting list from top to bottom. She sees at once which items have arrived, which are late and which need a gentle reminder.
At school, many families have not yet returned the trip forms, and Amara cannot remember which ones. She writes the names on her waiting list and ticks them off as the papers arrive.
Mr Bell has promised to fit a new lock on the library window, but he is busy with other repairs. Amara adds the lock to her list with a date, so that she can ask politely in a week.
Dev also keeps a waiting list, and he is surprised how long it is. He is waiting for his tutor's answer, for a library book and for a friend to lend him some notes.
When the date has passed, a short and friendly message is enough. Something like “Hello, I wanted to check whether the visit is still on for this week, and thank you” is polite, clear and kind.
On Wednesday afternoon, the plumber arrives at the door with his toolbox. Amara crosses the line off her waiting list, and the leak leaves her mind at the same moment as it leaves the kitchen.
In the hall hangs a big wall calendar with a square for every day. It is the right place for anything that must happen on one particular day or at one particular time.
Amara phones the dentist and books Zuri's check-up for a Thursday afternoon. She writes the day and the hour in the right square, and then she crosses the job off her list.
A calendar is not a to-do list, so do not fill it with hopes. Amara looks at her old calendar and sees that it is crowded with notes like start the report and tidy the shed.
When a calendar is full of maybes, you stop trusting it, because most of the notes are never done. Soon you ignore the whole thing, including the dates that truly matter.
A clean calendar has only a few clear marks and a lot of empty space. It tells the truth, and you can trust it at a glance.
The deadline for the school trip form goes on the calendar in bold pen, along with the day of the trip. Deadlines belong there because they are fixed, but wishes and hopes do not.
A reminder that is tied to one day may go on that day, such as post Mum's gift by Thursday. It is not a task for any day, but a note that you will see at the right moment.
Kofi's early shifts change from week to week, so Amara writes them in a column on the calendar. Now she knows which mornings she will be alone with Zuri and the cereal.
You may prefer a wall calendar, or one on your phone, but you should choose only one. For anything important, set an alarm, so that you never depend on your memory.
At the end of the week, Amara looks at her calendar and smiles. There are only six marks on the whole month, and each of them is true.
Some goals need more than one step, and these are called projects. Amara looks at a line that says gift for Mother, and she feels stuck, because it is too big for one job.
The first move is to write the result as a full sentence. Amara writes, Mother's gift bought, wrapped and posted by the twentieth, and now she knows exactly what done looks like.
Under the sentence, she lists every step that she can think of. They are ask Kofi for ideas, choose a gift, buy it, find a box and post it, and she underlines the first.
You do not need to plan every step in detail, because the future will change the plan anyway. Only the first step must be ready to do today, and the others can wait their turn.
The school trip is a project too, and Amara has handled it badly so far. She writes the result at the top, then lists the forms, the money and the names, and the muddle becomes a plan.

In a crowded lecture hall, Dev hears the professor mention an unexpected connection that could become the centre of his essay. Rather than clinging to it and missing the next ten minutes of the talk, he taps a short line into his phone and lets the thought go. He leaves the lecture with his notes in order and his attention still intact, which is rare for any student.

Kofi cannot write while driving a bus through the morning traffic, nor would anyone wish him to, so he adopts the method in his own way. When he reaches the depot for his break, he speaks each thought into his phone, and later that evening he copies the notes into a notebook of his own. The tool is slightly different, but the principle behind it remains exactly the same.

Ines, who walks briskly along the hospital corridors with a dozen demands on her time, still finds a quiet moment to scribble in her small notebook. She jots down the supplies that the ward is running short of, along with her own errands, such as a prescription and a birthday card. Her patients never notice, and neither does anyone else, but her mind remains wonderfully clear.

One night, about a week into the experiment, Amara wakes at two in the morning with a sudden memory of a form that she never wrote down. She lies there for an hour, rehearsing it and worrying that she will forget it again, and the old tiredness creeps back. It is a small failure, but it teaches her more about the method than any amount of explanation could.

This simple habit is the foundation on which every other part of the method rests, and without it the rest is only decoration. Whatever comes into your mind, whether it is large or small, serious or silly, urgent or merely curious, goes straight into the notebook. Once you trust that nothing will be lost, your mind will finally agree to stop guarding the door.

A long list, however carefully written, is not yet a plan, and it can feel every bit as heavy as the disorder it replaced. On Monday evening Amara sits down again at the kitchen table, with her sheet in front of her, and prepares to sort it one line at a time. This stage, she is beginning to see, is where the real work of the method is done.

For each item she asks a single question, which is whether there is anything she actually needs to do about it. The question sounds almost too simple to be useful, but it divides the list at once into the things that need her attention and the things that merely occupy her mind. Sometimes, she notices with some surprise, the honest answer is simply no, and then the item can simply be released.

When the answer is no, Amara allows herself to throw the note away, and she finds the permission strangely thrilling. She tears out the line about buying a new kettle, because the old one works perfectly well, and she drops the scrap into the wastebasket with a satisfying whisper. It is remarkable how many items on a list are there only because nobody has ever questioned them.

A number of her notes turn out to be pleasant possibilities rather than duties, such as a pottery class, a knitting course and a weekend by the sea. She would hate to lose them, but she also does not wish them to clutter her working list, so she copies each one onto a separate page that she calls her ideas page. There they can wait without nagging at her, rather like seeds that are kept safely in a packet until spring.

The ideas page does not demand daily attention, because nothing on it is urgent and nothing on it will spoil. Amara decides to read it once a week, at a time when she can enjoy dreaming and perhaps move one of the ideas into real life. In the meantime, the knowledge that her wishes are safe lets her stop circling around them in her thoughts.

Some of the notes are not tasks at all but facts that she may need to look up one day, such as the times of Zuri's swimming lessons and the number of the dentist. Such information, which might be called reference, belongs in a folder rather than on a list, because there is nothing to do with it except find it when it is needed. Mixing the two kinds together only makes the working list longer, noisier and a great deal harder to trust.

Amara empties a drawer in the hall and arranges a few plain folders inside it, labelled with simple words such as tickets, bills and manuals. Anything that she may need to look up, from the guarantee of the washing machine to a map of the swimming pool, now has an obvious home. The drawer is not exciting, but it is where she will never have to hunt for anything again.

By the end of the evening, Amara has thrown away about twenty items from the sheet, and she is amazed at how much lighter she feels for it. They were things that no longer mattered, things that somebody else had already done and things that she had never really intended to do. Letting them go is rather like clearing out an overstuffed cupboard and discovering the floor beneath.

Elsewhere in town, Dev tries the same exercise on his own list of forty items, spread across his desk in the corner of the library. Twelve of them turn out to belong to the essay, six are ideas that can wait, and the rest he cheerfully drops into the bin. Within a few minutes, his mountain has shrunk to something that looks much more like a hill.

When Amara looks up, three small stacks have formed on the table, one for things to do, one for ideas and one for things to keep. The first stack is far shorter than the sheet she began with, and every item in it now has a clear claim on her attention. Her next task is to decide, for each of them, what the first small step would be.

On Amara's list, the single word dentist sits like a small grey cloud, and it tells her nothing about what she is supposed to do. Every time she reads it, she feels a faint twinge of guilt, and then she turns away from it and does something easier. Vague notes are the ones we avoid, because the mind cannot begin a task that it cannot picture.

The cure for this vagueness is a question that you put to each item in turn, which is what the very first physical action would be. It might be to open an email, pick up a phone or look in a drawer, but it is always something that you could do with your hands in the next few minutes. The answer is nearly always smaller, simpler and far less frightening than the vague worry that was sitting on the page.

Begin every step with an action word, such as call, write, buy, ask or find, so that the line tells you precisely what to do without a moment's thought. A note that says dentist is merely a worry in disguise, whereas a note that says call the dentist is a job that anyone could pick up. The difference is slight on the page, but it is enormous in the mind, which loves a clear instruction and dreads a mystery.

Amara works down her list with a fresh pen and rewrites ten of the vaguest items as plain, active steps. Dentist becomes call the dentist for Zuri, gift becomes ask Kofi for ideas and trip form becomes read and sign the trip form. She feels as though she were turning grey fog into a row of clear signposts.

If a step still feels heavy, she should make it smaller until it seems almost silly, because resistance melts when a task is tiny. Instead of booking the appointment, Amara writes find the dentist's phone number, and the dread that had surrounded the whole business suddenly disappears. A step that you can finish in thirty seconds is a step that you will actually take.

For the leak, the first step is not to repair it, because Amara has no idea how to do that and no wish to learn this week. She writes find a plumber's number, and underneath she adds call him at lunch, so that the task is divided into two pieces that each fit easily into a spare moment. A problem that seemed to need a whole weekend now needs about three minutes.

Zuri's swimming kit also shrinks to a single small action, which is to look in the swim bag by the door. Amara realises that she has been worrying for days about goggles that may well be at the bottom of the bag, and that if they are not there, then the next step will be perfectly obvious. Until she looks, however, she cannot know what the problem really is, and no amount of worrying will tell her.

She has no idea what to give her mother, and in the past this uncertainty has made her put off the whole matter until the last minute. This time she does not write buy a present, because that is a whole project in disguise, but ask Kofi for two ideas, which she can finish at the kitchen table that very evening. What had seemed an impossible puzzle has become something that fits neatly into an ordinary evening conversation with her partner.

Many steps are so small that they take only a minute or two to finish, and these are best gathered together and done in a single short burst. On Tuesday morning, before the kettle has finished boiling, Amara texts the plumber's number to her phone, signs the trip form and finds her mother's address. Three jobs have vanished from the list in less time than it would have taken to worry about one.

With a bold pen, Amara draws a line through each finished job, and she is surprised by how much pleasure the small gesture gives her. Each crossed-out line is a tiny proof that the method works, and that her list is not a pile of guilt but a map of things that are getting done. For the first time in weeks, she looks at her notebook and feels in control.

On Wednesday morning, the plumber promises that he will come next week, but he gives no particular day, and he is gone before Amara can ask. She thanks him, then stands in the hall with a familiar sinking feeling, because she knows that a vague promise of this kind can easily slip out of both their minds. Left to her old habits, she would carry the worry around with her for days, and probably wake with it at three in the morning.

Many of the steps in our lives do not belong to us at all, because they depend on somebody else to do something first. For these, it helps to keep a separate list, which Amara calls the waiting list, and which is simply a record of everything that other people have promised or still owe her. It is a humble idea, but it is one of the pieces that makes the whole system hold together.

Each entry on the waiting list needs only three small facts, which are what you are waiting for, who owes it to you and the date on which you asked. Amara's first line reads plumber, visit, asked Wednesday, and it takes her about five seconds to write. Once the line is on the page, it no longer needs to live in her head.

Without a list of this kind, you carry every pending promise around in your mind, where it nags in exactly the same way as a task that you have forgotten to do. The waiting list allows you to put the matter down until a particular date and to trust that you will see it again. It is the difference between holding a heavy bag and putting it in a cloakroom with a ticket.

On Friday afternoon, Amara looks over the waiting list from top to bottom and notices at once which items have arrived, which are late and which need a gentle reminder. In the past, she would never have known that the dentist's confirmation was overdue, because she had no way of seeing what was missing. Now the gaps show up as clearly as holes in a row of buttons.

At school, the trip forms are trickling in slowly, and Amara has no idea which families have returned them and which have not. She writes the names on her waiting list, ticks them off as the slips of paper arrive and finds that the work, which usually causes her a nagging headache, is calm and almost pleasant. Even a large and untidy matter becomes calm and manageable when it has a proper list, and the pile of paper stops feeling like an accusation.

Mr Bell, the caretaker, has promised to fix the library window with a new lock, but he is busy with a flooded corridor and a broken heater, and nobody would blame him for forgetting. Amara adds the lock to her waiting list with a date a week ahead, so that she can ask him politely when the time comes. She no longer has to wonder, at midnight, whether the window is still open.

Dev has a waiting list of his own, and he is startled by how long it turns out to be, which tells him a good deal about why his mind has felt so crowded. He is waiting for his tutor to reply about his question, for a library book to be returned by someone else and for Lucas to lend him some notes. Seeing the three items together, he realises that none of them requires him to do anything at all.

When a date passes and nothing has arrived, a short and friendly message is almost always enough to move things forward. A message such as “Hello, I just wanted to check that everything is still on for this week, and thank you for your help” can be written in a few moments and carries no hint of blame. People rarely resent a polite reminder, and many are quietly grateful for it, because they too have heads that are full.

On Wednesday afternoon, a full week later, the plumber knocks on the door with his toolbox in one hand and a cheerful apology in the other. Amara crosses the line off her waiting list with a flourish, and the leak leaves her mind at the very moment that it leaves the kitchen. It is a small victory, but she realises that for the first time in months she did not have to chase anything alone.

In the hall of Amara's house hangs a large wall calendar, with a square for every day, and she decides to treat it with a new kind of respect. It is the right place for anything that must happen on one particular day or at one particular hour, such as an appointment, a lesson or a deadline. It is not the right place for anything else, and that is the point.

Amara phones the dentist and books Zuri's check-up for a Thursday afternoon at the end of the month, and she writes the day and the hour in the correct square with a firm hand. Then she crosses the job off her list, because the thing that remains, going to the appointment, belongs to the calendar and will appear there on its own. It is a small act of tidiness, and it brings her a strange satisfaction.

A calendar is not a to-do list, and the surest way to destroy its usefulness is to fill its squares with good intentions. When Amara looks at her old calendar from last year, she finds scribbles such as start the report and tidy the shed written in many different squares, none of which was ever done. Each of them is a small lie that the calendar told her, and a reason to doubt it.

Once a calendar is full of maybes and shoulds, you learn to ignore it, because experience has taught you that most of what it says is untrue. The danger is that you will start to ignore the true entries as well, such as the day that the passport must be renewed or the afternoon that a friend is arriving on the train. A calendar that cannot be trusted is, in the end, worse than having no calendar at all.

A clean calendar looks almost empty, with a few clear marks standing out against a great deal of white space, and that is exactly how it ought to look. Every mark on it is a promise that the day will hold something fixed, and the blank squares are a quiet reassurance that nothing else is hiding there. You can read it at a glance, and for the first time you believe what it says.

The date of the school trip goes on the calendar in a bold, dark pen, together with the day by which the forms must be returned. Deadlines belong on the calendar because they are fixed by someone else and cannot be moved by wishing, whereas a hope to start something early is only a hope and should sit on a list. Amara notices how clearly the difference shows once she has decided where to draw the line between them.

Occasionally there is something that is not an appointment but that you must see on one particular day, such as a note to post her mother's gift by Thursday. This kind of reminder can safely go on the date it belongs to, because it is tied to that day and no other, and the calendar will show it to you at the right moment. Such reminders must still be rare, or the calendar will slowly fill up with notes again.

Kofi's early shifts change from week to week, and until now Amara has only discovered them when his alarm woke her in the dark. She now writes them in a neat column down the side of the calendar, so that she can see at a glance which mornings she will be alone with Zuri and the breakfast. Knowing what is coming allows her to plan around it instead of being surprised.

It does not matter whether you prefer a calendar on the wall or one on your phone, but it does matter that you choose only one and use it faithfully. For anything important, set an alarm to ring a little ahead of time, so that you never depend on your memory to notice that the hour is approaching. Two calendars will always disagree sooner or later, and one of them will always turn out to be wrong.

At the end of the week, Amara stands in the hall and looks at the wall calendar, which now has only a handful of marks on the whole month. Each of them is a real appointment or a real deadline, and there is no longer a single entry that she does not believe. It looks bare, but it feels like a clean window through which the future can be seen clearly.

Some goals are too large to be a single step, and for these we use a word that sounds grander than it is, which is a project. It simply means any result that needs more than one action to complete, and Amara's list turns out to be full of them. A line that reads gift for Mother makes her feel stuck, because the line is a destination and not a step on the road.

The first move with any project is to write the result as a complete sentence, so that you know precisely what it will look like when it is finished. Amara writes, Mother's gift bought, wrapped and posted by the twentieth, and the vague worry of the last fortnight suddenly acquires a shape. Once you can describe the finish line, you can start to see the path towards it.

Beneath the sentence, she writes down every step that she can think of, in no particular order, and then she puts them into a sensible sequence. They are ask Kofi for ideas, choose a gift, buy it, find a box and post it, and she draws a firm line under the first one. The whole thing, which had loomed over her for a fortnight, now fits on three lines of her notebook.

You do not have to plan every step in detail, because the real world will change the plan before you reach the end of it. All that matters is that the first step is clear and ready to be taken today, and that the others are waiting in line behind it. A project is not a plan carved in stone, but a path that you light one lamp at a time.

The school trip is a project too, although until now Amara has handled it as a vague and rather alarming cloud of paper. She writes the result at the top of a fresh page, which is that every child has a signed form and a payment by the Friday, and then she lists the steps beneath. The muddle becomes a plan, and the plan fits comfortably on one side of the page.

Parents' evening is another project that has been sitting on her mind, and it contains a good many small pieces, from the letters to the room to the rows of chairs. Amara writes each piece as a separate step and adds a line on her waiting list that reads Mr Bell, chairs, asked Monday. She is pleased to notice that the whole event has stopped feeling like a mountain.

Amara decides to keep one page in her notebook that lists all her projects, so that none of them can hide in the corners of her memory. A project that is not written anywhere will sit quietly in the back of your mind, using up a little energy every day, and then suddenly leap out at you when it is almost too late. The page works like a roll call, in which every project must answer to its name.

When she counts the lines on her project page, Amara finds that she has fourteen of them, which is far more than she had imagined. Some are large, such as the school trip, and some are small, such as the new shoes for Zuri, but together they have been sitting in her head for months. It is no wonder that she has been so tired, and she smiles to think that she carried them all without a single note.

A project that has no next step beside it is not really a project at all, but only a wish, and so she runs her finger down the page checking each line. Wherever a step is missing, she writes one, even if the step is only to ask someone for advice or to look something up on the library computer. The effect is to turn a page of vague good intentions into a list of things that can be started.

On Thursday, Amara carries the wrapped parcel to the post office, queues politely behind two other customers and sends it off with a tracking slip that she tucks into her purse. A week later, her mother telephones in a state of great delight to say that the gift is exactly what she wanted, and Amara hangs up with a glow of pride. Then she turns to her notebook, draws a line through the whole project and feels how good it is to finish something.

Dev, a university student, has been given a long essay on how rivers shaped the first cities, and the deadline is three weeks away. He sits in the library with a blank page in front of him, and the empty screen seems to expand with every minute that he avoids it. The more he thinks about the whole mountain, the less able he is to take the first step up.

Rather than starting, Dev tidies his desk, rearranges his pens and wanders off to buy a coffee that he does not especially want. He knows perfectly well that he is avoiding the work, and the guilt this brings makes the task seem even heavier than before. It is a familiar cycle, in which avoidance feeds dread and dread feeds more avoidance.

That evening, his flatmate Lucas, who has noticed the pile of untouched books, puts a mug of tea beside the laptop and offers some simple advice. He tells Dev to write down everything he knows about the subject, everything he fears about it and everything that he still needs to find out. There is no need to organise anything, Lucas says, because the page is only a place to put the noise.

Dev fills a whole page in fifteen minutes, and he is startled to find that the fears take up more space than the facts. Then, at the top of a fresh page, he writes a single sentence that describes the finish, which is a completed essay of about four thousand words, handed in with time to spare. Seeing the goal in plain ink makes it feel less like a threat and more like an agreement.

Beneath the sentence, he lists the big steps in order, which are to choose a question, to read three good sources, to make a plan, to write the parts and to edit the whole. None of them looks frightening on its own, although together they once seemed to make a wall. The trick, he sees, is to stop looking at the wall and to start looking at the first brick.

Dev copies each of the steps onto an index card and arranges the cards in a row on a library table, where the autumn light falls across them. If he decides that the order is wrong, he can simply move a card, which is so much easier than rewriting a list or rethinking a vague plan. The cards give his thoughts a physical shape that he can pick up, shuffle and put down.

His first small step is not to write a word of the essay, but to send an email to his tutor, Dr Moyo, asking whether his chosen question is a good one. The email takes six minutes, and he feels better the moment he presses send, as though a window had opened in a stuffy room. Even though not a single sentence of the essay has been written, the whole project has begun to move at last.

Dr Moyo replies the next day, in a friendly and rather brisk way, and suggests a narrower and clearer question than the one Dev had proposed. Dev is relieved, because a smaller question means fewer sources to read and a much shorter road to the end. He writes the new question on a card, puts it at the front of the row and crosses the line off his waiting list with some satisfaction.

Dev now divides the essay into ten parts of about four hundred words each, and he treats every part as a small project with its own sentence and its own steps. Four hundred words is an amount that anyone can imagine writing in a morning, whereas four thousand words is a number that makes the stomach turn. By changing the size of the task, he has changed how it feels to begin.

After a week, the mountain has turned into a path, and Dev no longer wakes up with a heavy feeling beneath his ribs. Each morning he looks at his cards, chooses a step and does it, and by the evening he can see that the whole row is a little closer to the end. The work is exactly as large as it was before, but now it can be carried one step at a time.

At lunch on Tuesday, Amara opens her notebook, looks at the long list of steps and finds that she cannot decide where to begin. Every line seems to demand attention, and so she ends up doing none of them, wasting twenty minutes on an apple and a worry. A list that is not organised can be as paralysing as a head that is not.

The solution is to group the small steps by the place or the tool that they need, and Amara draws up three short headings on a card, which are calls, errands and computer. She copies each step under the right heading, so that her single heavy list breaks into three light ones. It is the same work, but it comes in pieces that a person can actually pick up.

When she goes out, she looks only at her errands, and she is delighted to find that the pharmacy, the post office and the library all stand within a few minutes of one another. She does the whole round in a single forty-minute walk, instead of making five separate trips on five separate days. Saving effort in this way feels almost like being given a present of free time, wrapped up in an ordinary walk.

On a quiet afternoon at her school desk, Amara makes her four telephone calls one after the other, while she is in the mood and the phone is already in her hand. It is easier to speak to strangers when you have just done it, and she has finished the lot before her coffee has had time to cool. The same four calls, spread over a week, would have cost her a dozen worries.

Her computer steps are saved for the moment she sits down at the school office computer, with a mug of tea and a clear half hour. She answers her emails, fills in a form and orders the paper for the copier, and she is spared the nagging fear that she might have missed something. Everything that needs a screen is now waiting for her in one place, and nothing else interrupts it.

Choosing what to do now becomes quite easy if you ask yourself four plain questions. How much time do I have, how much energy have I got, where am I and what tools do I have with me, and what matters most? The answers usually point to a single step that you can take without hesitation.

After lunch, Amara has only fifteen minutes and very little energy, because the morning has been busy and the afternoon looks long. She glances at her list of calls, chooses the two easiest and finishes them with time to spare, feeling a small glow of achievement. She does not try to attempt the hard step, because on a day like this it would only make her miserable.

Dev has noticed that he thinks best in the morning, and he has learned to protect those hours for the hardest writing, leaving the rest of the day for lighter work. In the afternoon, when he is tired, he renames files, orders books and sorts the references into a neat list, which are all useful jobs that need no brilliance. By matching the task to the energy, he gets far more done than before.

When you trust your lists, choosing what to do takes seconds and not an afternoon of wandering, because you no longer have to argue with yourself. You know that everything is written down somewhere safe, so you can give your whole attention to one thing without fear that another is slipping away. The freedom that this brings is, perhaps, the real reward of the whole method, and it arrives sooner than you might expect.

Amara closes her notebook with a satisfied nod and walks back to her desk with an easy step. She has understood that the aim of all this is not to do everything, which is impossible, but to choose well among the things that can be done at this moment. A life managed with such care may still be busy, but it is no longer crowded with fear.

A list is useful only if you trust it, and you will trust it only if you look at it regularly, which means that even the best system will fail if it is allowed to gather dust. Amara therefore decides to build a small habit around her notebook, a kind of daily handshake with her own plans. It must be so short that she cannot find a reason to skip it.

Every morning, before the household gets busy, Amara sits down at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and her notebook, and she spends five minutes on a short daily look. The time is brief enough that it feels almost like a moment of rest, and yet it shapes everything that follows. It takes less time than reading the news, and it is a good deal more useful.

First she opens the calendar and notes what is fixed for today, such as appointments, meetings, lessons and deadlines. These things cannot be moved, so she plans around them as a gardener plants around a wall, and she gives them her full attention before anything else. Knowing exactly where the boundaries lie makes the rest of the day much easier to arrange and enjoy.

Next she reads through her lists and chooses the two or three things that matter most, and she writes them on a card in front of her. She does not try to select everything, because a short plan is a plan that can actually be kept, whereas a long one is merely a wish. If she manages those few things, she will count the day as a success.

After that, she checks the waiting list for anything that is due or overdue, and writes a quick message if some matter has dragged on too long. It takes less than a minute, and it gives her a quiet confidence that nobody is being forgotten and nothing is silently going wrong. What used to be a quiet source of worry has become nothing more than a small and rather pleasant chore.

Finally, she gathers any loose notes from her pockets, her handbag and the back of her coat, and writes them into the notebook before the day begins. By the time her tea is finished, everything is in one place, the day has a rough shape and she knows what she has promised herself. In the space of five minutes, a morning that might have been a muddle has been turned into something like a map.

On her very first morning, Kofi has already left for the depot, and Zuri sits across the table, eating her cereal and swinging her feet. Amara opens her notebook, reads her list in near silence, and by the time the bowl is empty she has a clear idea of how the day will go. Zuri watches with curiosity but does not interrupt, as if she knew that something important was happening.

At school, Hana, the head teacher, puts her head round the office door and asks for the list of trip forms that have still not come in. Amara knows exactly where it is, and passes it across the desk in a few seconds, and Hana looks both pleased and slightly surprised. It is a small moment, but it shows how a few minutes of care can pay off in the middle of a busy day.

Around lunchtime, Amara takes one more short look at the card that she wrote in the morning, which takes less than a minute and requires no special effort. This small pause is enough to keep the afternoon on its course and to prevent small things from sliding away unnoticed while she is busy with something else. It works like a glance at a map in the middle of a journey.

Plans change, of course, and a surprise can ruin even the neatest morning, as every parent knows who has been called away by a sudden telephone call. A clear list cannot prevent the surprise, but it does allow you to change your plan calmly, because you can see everything that is at stake and you can choose the next best thing. A good plan, in the end, is one that can bend a little without breaking, and the daily look keeps it supple.

A short daily look is enough to keep a person afloat, but small messes still pile up quietly behind it, like dust in the corners of a room. By the end of her first week, Amara finds that her notebook contains old notes, loose scraps of paper and several lines that are no longer true. A system needs sweeping now and then, or it will slowly lose her trust.

She therefore chooses a regular time for a larger tidy, and she settles on Friday afternoon, when the working week is winding down. She sits at the kitchen table with a lamp lit, a cup of tea at her elbow and the notebook open, and she calls the ritual her end-of-week tidy. It is a quiet hour that she soon begins to look forward to, rather than one that she dreads.

The first step is to empty her pockets, her handbag and her coat onto the table, and to enter every scrap that she finds into the notebook. Receipts, torn envelopes and notes scribbled on the back of a bus ticket are each given a line or thrown away, so that nothing stays loose in the corners of her life. The pile is never large, but she is always strangely relieved to watch it vanish from the table.

Second, she empties her head once more, writing down whatever has appeared in the course of the week, just as she did on that first Sunday evening. There are always a few things, such as a gift to buy, a form to find or a worry that she had not noticed, and they are far easier to catch on Friday than to carry through the weekend. The page grows shorter every week, which is a sign that the habit of writing things down at once is working.

Third, she looks back at last week's calendar to see whether anything was left unfinished, and then she looks three weeks ahead so that no appointment can take her by surprise. A glance forward is rather like checking the weather before a journey, and it often shows her a deadline that she should begin to prepare for. Because the calendar has been kept clean and honest, this glance backwards and forwards takes her only a minute or two.

Fourth, she goes through her lists with a pen, ticking off what is finished, rewording what is vague and removing everything that has gone stale or become untrue. A list that contains only live and honest entries is a list that she will want to open, whereas one that is cluttered with ghosts will soon be ignored. The tearing out of an old and finished page, and the sound that it makes, is oddly and quietly satisfying.

Fifth, she reads the waiting list from top to bottom and writes two short messages to people whose promises are overdue, using the friendly wording that she has now learned. It takes her only a couple of minutes, and the knowledge that those requests are on their way spares her several small worries over the weekend. Nothing is left to hang unanswered in the air, and nobody is left wondering whether they have been forgotten.

Sixth, she turns to the page where her projects are listed and checks that every one of them has a first step written beside it, clear enough to start at once. Where a step is missing, she supplies one, even if it is only to ask someone for advice, because a project without a next step is a wish and will go nowhere. This is the stage that keeps the whole machine moving, because it turns every wish on the page into a direction.

Seventh, she opens her ideas page and reads it with unconcealed pleasure, as one might enjoy a seed catalogue in midwinter. One idea she moves onto her active list, because the time now seems right, and another she crosses out, because she finds that she no longer cares about it. The page is a small garden that she is free to prune and to plant again whenever she likes.

The whole tidy takes about an hour, and when it is finished Amara feels a light and spacious calm that she has not known for years. She switches off the lamp, closes the notebook, carries her cup to the sink and walks out into the weekend with a mind that has nothing hidden in its corners. A clear Friday, she has begun to see, is the beginning of a better Monday.

In the middle of dinner, with the soup half eaten and Zuri telling a long story about a classmate, Amara suddenly remembers a form that must be signed. In the past she would have lost the rest of the conversation to the worry, nodding politely while her mind raced elsewhere. Now she takes out the pen, writes three words in her notebook and returns to the table with her attention unharmed.

Zuri looks curiously at her mother's pen, and Kofi, across the table, only smiles, because he has long since learned that the habit takes about five seconds. Nobody feels ignored, and the story continues just where it left off, with a little more laughter than before. It is surprising how little a note costs when it saves the attention of everyone present.

Your email is simply another place where things gather, and left alone it becomes a second head, crowded with other people's demands and half-remembered promises. The answer is to deal with it in batches, at planned times, and to treat every message as a note that needs a decision. You are not obliged to answer a message at the very moment that it arrives, however urgent the sender may make it sound.

For each message in the pile you have four possible choices, and nothing more is ever required of you. You can delete it, reply at once if the reply takes only a minute, file it away for later reference, or turn it into a clear step in your notebook and then leave it. Having only four options makes the decision fast, because there is no longer any room for brooding.

At the school office, Amara opens an inbox that holds sixty unread messages, a sight that would once have ruined her morning. She works through them in order for twenty minutes, deleting some, answering others in a line and turning a few into steps, and when she looks up, only a handful remain. The mountain was made of small stones, and each of them was lighter than she feared.

Amara goes into the settings of her phone and turns off nearly all the alerts, the buzzes and the little red circles that used to pull her away from whatever she was doing. The messages still arrive, and she misses nothing that really matters, but now she chooses the moment when she looks at them. It is rather like closing a door against the noise of the street while keeping the window open for the air.

She decides to read her email at fixed times, such as ten in the morning and three in the afternoon, and to ignore it in between with a clear conscience. The hours between are used for one thing at a time, and she finds that her work is both faster and better, since she is no longer interrupted every few minutes. Nobody has complained about the change, and she has so far missed nothing that could not wait for a few hours.

After a meeting, when the memory of the decisions is still bright, Amara spends two minutes writing down exactly what was agreed and, above all, what her own first steps are. Without this habit, she knows from experience, the conclusions of a meeting dissolve in an hour, leaving everyone with a different memory of what was promised. Those two minutes, spent while everyone is still in the room, are among the most valuable of her entire working week.

Paper arrives as well, in the form of letters through the door, notices in her daughter's school bag and forms from the office, and it needs a system as much as email does. Amara sets up a single tray on the kitchen shelf, puts every piece of paper into it and sorts it once a day in the same way, as a note, a step, a fact to file or a bin. The tray never overflows, because she empties it faithfully every afternoon, and so the kitchen shelf stays clear and calm.

What all these cases have in common is that whatever arrives, whether a thought, a message, a form or a request, goes to one place first and is sorted afterwards. Nothing is allowed to hover in the air, demanding attention in a hundred small ways, because everything has a home to go to while it waits for a decision. This is the quiet principle behind the whole method, and it works wherever life delivers something new.

Over the course of an ordinary day we make hundreds of small choices, from what to wear and what to eat to when to leave and which road to take. Each decision costs a little attention, and when they are all made fresh every day, they can leave us feeling oddly tired by the evening. Some of them, however, come back in exactly the same form again and again, and these are the ones that can be decided once.

For Amara, Mondays have become the day of one routine decision, and the decision is what the family will eat. She sits down with a pencil, writes the week's dinners in a column from Monday to Sunday and sticks the page to the fridge with a magnet, where everyone can see it. The question that used to ambush her at six o'clock every evening has been answered in advance.

From the plan, she writes a shopping list in a few minutes, and the whole week's food can be bought in one trip instead of a dozen small and hurried ones. She no longer stands in front of the open fridge asking herself what to cook, and she no longer finds herself, at the last moment, with eggs and nothing else. The money saved is certainly useful, but the attention that she saves each evening is worth a good deal more.

On Friday evening, Zuri and her mother pack the swimming bag together, with the towel, the goggles and a clean costume, and they place it by the front door, ready for the morning. When Saturday arrives, there is no frantic hunt through drawers and no tears about a missing cap, and the lesson begins calmly. A small routine, repeated every week without fuss, has quietly removed a whole category of trouble from the household.

Kofi has a routine of his own, because getting out of the house before five in the morning is hard enough without searching for lost keys in the dark. Every night he lays out his uniform, his badge and his keys on the chair, so that the early start is almost automatic and he can move through it half asleep. The most important decisions, he says with a grin, are those that you do not have to make at four thirty.

Dev decides that he will write every morning from nine until eleven, in the same corner of the same library, and he treats the habit as an appointment with himself. He no longer has to ask each day whether he feels like starting, because the clock has quietly settled the question, and the effort that he saves goes into the sentences themselves. His essay grows steadily, one quiet morning after another, and he is surprised how soon he begins to enjoy the hours.

Even the school office now runs on routines, because Hana, who likes to keep things calm and fair, has given every regular job its own day of the week. Forms are sent out on Tuesday and collected on Friday, the noticeboard is changed on Monday morning and nobody has to remember anything at all. The order brings a peaceful rhythm to a place that was once always in a hurry.

A routine is not a cage, and it should never be allowed to become one, because its only purpose is to save effort for the things that matter. When a friend invites the family to dinner on a Wednesday, Amara simply swaps one meal for another on her plan, and nothing is lost or spoiled. A system that cannot bend, however neat it looks, is a system that sooner or later will be abandoned.

You do not need to rebuild your whole life at once, and it would be unwise to try, since habits grow best when they are small and few. Choose a single routine for this coming week, such as the dinners, the school bag, the clothes or the hour in which you will do your most important work, and then test it for seven days. If it helps, keep it, and if it does not, change it without guilt.

By Thursday, Amara has noticed something quietly delightful, which is that one decision made on Monday has saved her about six small decisions later in the week. Her evenings feel calmer and her mind is lighter, and the family eats better than it has for months, with less fuss and no argument. She wonders how many other questions in her life could be answered once and then left alone.

By the third week of the experiment, Amara's list has quietly grown to more than eighty items, and she can feel the old heaviness creeping back into her shoulders. A system that collects everything faithfully has one danger, which is that it can make you aware of exactly how much you have promised. If your list is too long, then you have promised too much, and the only remedy is honesty.

The test is simple, and you can apply it to each line in turn, which is to ask whether you will really do the thing in the next three months. If the honest answer is no, take the item off your active list, and either throw it away or move it to the ideas page, where it can wait without nagging. This is not failure or laziness, but simply good housekeeping, of the kind that any busy household needs now and then.

Amara writes down roughly how long each of her steps would take and then adds up the hours, an exercise that she has avoided for years because she suspected the answer. As she feared, she has many more hours of tasks than she has hours in a week, and the shock explains why she has always felt that she was running behind. The list itself was never the problem, but the sum of all her promises certainly was, and now she can see it clearly.

Every yes that we give is also a quiet no to something else, and that something is usually rest, family or the work that matters most to us. If Amara agrees to join another long committee on Thursday evenings, she is silently agreeing to give up those evenings with Zuri and Kofi, and she must decide whether the exchange is worth it. Seen like this, as an exchange rather than a simple favour, the choice becomes far clearer and a good deal easier to make.

One afternoon at school, a colleague arrives at her desk with a folder and asks whether Amara could take over a large piece of work that she cannot manage herself. Amara looks at her list, thinks about the days ahead, and then, with a gentle smile, she shakes her head. It is not easy, because she has always hated to disappoint anyone, but she finds the words come more readily than she expected.

A kind no has three simple ingredients, which are thanks for the request, a short and truthful reason and, where possible, a helpful suggestion about who else might be able to say yes. Amara tells her colleague that she would love to help, but that her week is already full, and she mentions the name of someone in the next room who has more time. The colleague smiles, thanks her for being straightforward, and goes off to ask the other person, and nobody at all is offended.

Sometimes the right answer is neither a yes nor a no but a not now, which postpones the matter honestly without closing the door. When a friend asks her to help with a stall at the summer fair, Amara replies that she cannot think about it until the school trip is over, and she writes that date on her waiting list. People accept a clear delay far more easily than a vague and anxious maybe.

Amara goes to see Hana and explains plainly that she has too much to do this week, and that she would like to talk about which tasks can wait. Hana, who has noticed the improvement in her work over recent weeks, nods at once and says that she would much rather hear an honest answer than receive a tired yes. The conversation lasts five minutes, and it removes a weight from both their shoulders.

The hardest person to refuse is often oneself, and Amara finds that her own wishes are the ones that crowd her list most stubbornly. She crosses the pottery class off her active list, not because she has lost interest in it, but because she knows that the autumn is full, and she writes it carefully on the ideas page instead. The wish is not destroyed but only postponed, and she feels no guilt about it.

With a lighter list, Amara finds that she has time for the things that never appear in any notebook, because they are the reason for having a notebook at all. On Sunday afternoon, she and Zuri walk to the park in the thin autumn sunshine and spend an hour feeding the ducks and talking about nothing in particular. It is exactly the kind of hour that the whole method was built to protect, and it is worth more than any tidy list.

Some items stay on a list for weeks without moving, and each time Amara reads them she feels a small pinch of discomfort. One line, which says write to Aunt Mary, has been sitting there for a full month, and she has begun to read around it as one steps around a puddle. A stuck item is not a sign of weakness, but a signal that something about it needs to be looked at.

When an item refuses to move, the most useful thing to do is to ask it why. Is the step too big, is it unclear, is it something that you no longer want, are you waiting for a decision, or is it merely unpleasant? Naming the reason usually takes less than a minute, and it points almost immediately to the cure.

If the job is too big, break it down into a first step that is so small that it is almost funny. Write to Aunt Mary becomes find a pen and a card, and on that same evening the card is lying on the kitchen table, waiting, with the address already beside it. Having begun the task in this humble way, she finds that the rest comes quickly.

If the job is unclear, you can pause to write a short sentence describing what finished would look like, in the same way that you would for a project. A clear picture of the end will often show you the first step that you were missing, and it removes the fog that makes you avoid the work. A surprising amount of what we call laziness is really nothing more than simple, honest confusion about what the task is.

If you discover that you no longer want to do the job at all, the honest course is to let it go, without guilt and without a long explanation. Amara crosses out an old promise to join a book group that she signed up for out of politeness, and she is amazed to find that the world goes on exactly as before. Some items on our lists are only the ghosts of promises that no longer matter.

A worry that keeps returning is far easier to carry when it has a step beside it, and Amara tries this on the one that has troubled her most. She writes that Zuri is afraid of deep water, and next to it, in a firm hand, ask the swimming teacher for advice, which is a small act that she can do on Saturday. The worry has not vanished, but it has become something that she can meet on a Saturday morning, and that is a great improvement.

The teacher turns out to be warm and sensible, and she suggests that Zuri should practise floating on her back in the shallow end, with a hand beneath her shoulders until she feels safe. At the next lesson, Zuri lies on the water for the first time with her ears underwater and her eyes on the ceiling, and her face is a picture of astonished joy. Amara, watching from the side, feels the old worry shrink to the size of a pebble.

There are worries that have no step at all, because they concern things that we cannot change, such as the weather, the economy or another person's choices. For these, Amara draws two short columns in her notebook, one headed what I can control and the other what I cannot, and she lets herself put down the second column for the evening. It does not make the trouble disappear, but it stops her from carrying it uphill.

Dev is stuck on the introduction to his essay, and every opening sentence that he writes seems clumsier than the last, so that he has now wasted three mornings. When he mentions it to Dr Moyo, she tells him with a smile to leave it until the very end, because it is far easier to introduce an essay that already exists than one that is only a hope. A week later, when the rest of the essay stands ready, he writes the introduction in twenty minutes and wonders what the fuss was about.

A difficult decision can become stuck too, especially when you are afraid of choosing wrongly and so choose nothing, and the matter circles round and round in your mind. A good remedy is to set a date by which you will decide, to write it on the calendar and to use the time between to collect whatever information you need. Once the date is fixed and written down, the question is allowed to rest in the notebook, and so, at last, are you.

At home, Amara and Kofi now share a shopping list on their phones, and a family calendar hangs on the fridge, and the arrangement has changed the quiet tension between them. Neither of them has to remember everything alone, and neither of them has to nag the other, because the information is there for both to see. A system shared with the people you love is lighter to carry than one kept in a single head.

The family calendar shows Kofi's early shifts, Zuri's swimming lessons, the dentist and every other fixed date in a different coloured pen for each person. Anyone can see at a glance where everybody will be, and nobody is taken by surprise by a lesson that was never mentioned or a shift that was changed without a word. It is a small thing, but it quietly removes dozens of tiny arguments that used to begin in the kitchen at breakfast.

On Sunday evening, the family sits at the kitchen table for ten minutes with a cup of tea and the notebook, and they look together at the week that is coming. Anyone may add an item to the list, and Zuri, who is nine, is allowed to suggest something that she would like to do on Saturday. These brief meetings are cheerful rather than solemn, and they prevent the quiet build-up of misunderstanding.

Zuri has a small list of her own, with drawings of her little jobs, such as feeding the fish, packing her school bag and putting her shoes by the door, and she ticks each one off with a coloured pencil. She is prouder of the ticks than of any sticker, and her mother notices that the morning rush has become calmer. Even a child of nine can feel the pleasure of a job that has been seen and finished.

When Amara asks someone else for help, she is careful to be clear about three things, which are who should do the job, exactly what the job is and by when it should be done. Then she writes it on her waiting list, so that she can follow up kindly if the day passes and nothing has happened. Asking clearly is a form of respect, because it spares the other person from guessing what is wanted.

At school, Mr Bell has seen how well Amara's lists work, and he pins a repair list to the board in the corridor, with a column for jobs done and another for those waiting. Everyone in the building can now see what has been reported, and teachers no longer stop him in the hall with half-remembered requests while he is carrying a ladder. He says, with a rare grin, that it is the best thing that has happened to his week.

One week, Zuri comes down with a bad cold and a fever, and Amara stays at home to nurse her, with nothing in her mind but soup and thermometers. The lists are forgotten, the calendar goes unread and the waiting list gathers dust, so that by Sunday the whole system has quietly fallen behind. It is exactly the kind of week in which any method might break, and for a moment she feels like a failure.

But Amara does not scold herself, because she knows that the system is not a test of her character, and that it has been designed to recover. On the next quiet evening, she sits down for an hour and empties her head once more, exactly as she did on that first Sunday, and sorts the result into steps and lists. In a single evening, the mess of a week is gone, and she feels the old calm return.

Dev, who is always eager for a better tool, tries three different apps in a single week and finds that he has spent far more time moving his notes around than writing his essay. At the end of the week, he goes back to the first one, which was perfectly adequate, and he resolves to leave it alone until the essay is finished. A plain tool that you use every day will always beat a perfect tool that you only admire.

Ines notices how calm Amara has become, and she asks her over the garden fence what has changed, since it is plain that something has. Amara invites her in for a cup of tea, shows her the notebook with its small fish drawn inside the cover and teaches her the five steps that she has learned, which Ines greets with delight. It seems that the teacher has become the student, and that the notebook has now crossed the fence.

At the end of the working day, shortly before six, Amara writes a brief note about tomorrow, closes her laptop and tidies her desk. It is a small ritual, rather like drawing the curtains at dusk, and it tells her whole body that the working day is over. Then she lets work go until the next morning, and she does not worry about it.

Her closing note is only three lines long, and she writes it in the same plain notebook, so that she can find it at once when she returns. It says where she stopped, what the very first step will be tomorrow and anything that is still open, such as a message that she is waiting for. In effect, she is leaving a letter for her future self, and the letter is always kind.

With the note safely written, her mind can leave the office behind, and she discovers that the walk home is no longer filled with the replaying of the day. She notices the colour of the sky, the smell of rain on the pavement and the shape of the trees, and she reaches her own front door with some energy still in reserve. This, more than any technique, is what she had hoped the method would give her.

One small study, carried out with a group of young adults, found that those who spent a few minutes writing a to-do list before bed fell asleep faster than those who wrote about what they had already done. The study was small, and more research is needed before anyone can be certain, but the result is easy to understand. A mind that has handed over its worries to paper has less to rehearse in the dark.

That night, Amara writes tomorrow's tasks on a small pad that she keeps beside the bed, and then she puts the pen down on top of it, turns off the light and closes her eyes. The house is quiet, the notebook is waiting at its hook by the door and nothing in her head is shouting for attention. For the first time in months, she sleeps peacefully, and the dawn finds her still dreaming.

A month later, Amara wakes in the soft light of a Saturday morning, rested and unhurried, and she lies for a moment listening to the birds. Her list is still long, because a full life never has a short one, but her nights are quiet, and the leak, the trip form, her mother's gift and Zuri's dentist visit are all finished. She feels as though she has been given back the part of herself that was always busy guarding things.

Dev finishes his essay two days before the deadline, which has never happened to him before, and he carries the pages to his tutor with a light and cheerful step. He says afterwards that the secret was not talent or hard work, but simply knowing exactly what to do next on every morning of the three weeks. Lucas cheers loudly in the corridor, and Dr Moyo, receiving the essay with a smile, looks as if she had never doubted him.

Here, then, is the whole system in five words, which are collect, sort, choose, review and rest. You collect everything that is in your head into one trusted place, you sort it into clear steps, you choose what to do now, you review your lists often, and then you allow your mind to rest. Everything else in this book is only a detail of one of those five.

You do not need to do everything today, and you should not try, because habits that begin too large tend to die before the week is out. Begin with ten minutes, a pen and a page, and write down whatever is on your mind, however trivial, until the flow stops of its own accord. That one small act, repeated again and again, is how every part of this method begins and how it grows.

So today, before the evening arrives, find a pen and a clean page and write down every single thing that is on your mind. Your head was made for noticing, imagining and deciding, and not for storing lists, so give it the rest that it has been asking for. A clear head leads to a clear day, and the first step towards both is a single line on an empty page.
